cards.t: Type 1 (T1DM) & Type 2 (T2DM)
cards.d: Type 1 diabetes: the immune system destroys the insulin-making beta cells, so the body makes little or no insulin. Type 2 diabetes: the body does not use insulin well (insulin resistance), and over time the pancreas cannot make enough to keep up.
w: Type 1 is caused by eating too much sugar and Type 2 is caused by too little exercise.
Type 1 and Type 2 both mean the kidneys stop making insulin.
Type 1 is temporary pregnancy diabetes and Type 2 is caused by a virus.
cards.e: Type 1 is autoimmune and usually starts in childhood or young adulthood. Type 2 is the most common form and is linked to weight, inactivity, and genetics.

cards.t: What is prediabetes?
cards.d: A condition in which blood sugar is higher than normal but not yet high enough to be diagnosed as type 2 diabetes. An A1C of 5.7 to 6.4 percent or a fasting glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL is in this range.
w: A type of diabetes that appears only after surgery.
Blood sugar below 70 mg/dL that happens after meals.
A condition in which the kidneys filter out all glucose.
cards.e: Prediabetes raises the risk of developing type 2 diabetes, and the CDC notes that losing 5 to 7 percent of body weight and being more active can reduce that risk.

cards.t: What is an A1C (What are the levels of an A1C)?
cards.d: A1C is a blood test that shows average blood sugar over about 2 to 3 months. Below 5.7 percent is normal, 5.7 to 6.4 percent is prediabetes, and 6.5 percent or higher is diabetes.
w: A1C is a urine test that counts ketones, and 5 percent or more means normal.
A1C is a daily fingerstick reading, and 200 mg/dL or higher means normal.
A1C is a blood pressure reading, and 120 over 80 is the diabetes level.
cards.e: The A1C reflects average glucose because red blood cells last about 3 months. The CDC lists the thresholds above.

cards.t: Diabetes complications
cards.d: Long-term high blood sugar can damage the heart and blood vessels, the eyes (retinopathy), the kidneys (nephropathy), the nerves (neuropathy), and the feet and skin, and it raises the risk of stroke and infections.
w: Diabetes complications are limited to tooth decay and hair loss.
Diabetes complications only affect the lungs and cause asthma.
Diabetes complications are harmless and do not change over time.
cards.e: Most complications come from years of high blood sugar damaging small and large blood vessels and nerves. Good control and regular screening lower the risk.

cards.t: Gestational diabetes & risk factors
cards.d: Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar that first appears during pregnancy. Risk factors include being overweight or having obesity, a family history of type 2 diabetes, being age 35 or older, a previous pregnancy with gestational diabetes or a large baby, and PCOS.
w: Gestational diabetes is caused by the baby producing sugar, and it has no risk factors.
Gestational diabetes only happens after delivery and is caused by eating fruit.
Gestational diabetes is linked only to being underweight and exercising daily.
cards.e: CDC lists these risk factors. Most people with gestational diabetes return to normal glucose after delivery, but they face a higher risk of type 2 diabetes later.

cards.t: What is the test called for gestational diabetes?
cards.d: The glucose challenge test and the glucose tolerance test (oral glucose tolerance test, OGTT). Screening usually happens between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy.
w: The urine culture, done at the first prenatal visit.
The ultrasound of the placenta, done at 40 weeks.
The hemoglobin electrophoresis, done after delivery.
cards.e: The glucose challenge test is a 1-hour screen after a sugary drink. A positive screen is followed by the 3-hour glucose tolerance test to confirm the diagnosis.

cards.t: How does gestational diabetes affect the fetus?
cards.d: Extra glucose crosses the placenta and makes the fetus produce extra insulin. This can cause macrosomia (a large baby), low blood sugar after birth, breathing problems, jaundice, and a higher risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes later in life.
w: It shrinks the fetus and stops the development of the brain before birth.
It has no effect on the fetus because glucose cannot cross the placenta.
It only causes the fetus to be born early with no other effect.
cards.e: Uncontrolled gestational diabetes increases risks for both the mother and the baby, so blood sugar is monitored and treated during pregnancy.
cards.s: NIDDK: Diabetes in America, Chapter 4 (Gestational Diabetes)

cards.t: Difference between hyper & hypoglycemia
cards.d: Hyperglycemia is blood sugar that is too high, usually above the target range set for the patient. Hypoglycemia is blood sugar that is too low, generally below 70 mg/dL.
w: Hyperglycemia is low blood pressure, and hypoglycemia is high blood pressure.
Hyperglycemia is a fever, and hypoglycemia is a cold.
They are two names for the same condition, both caused by eating too much protein.
cards.e: High blood sugar can cause thirst, frequent urination, and fatigue. Low blood sugar can cause shakiness, sweating, confusion, and can be an emergency if severe.

cards.t: What is the treatment for hypoglycemia?
cards.d: For a conscious patient, give 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate (such as 4 ounces of juice or glucose tablets), recheck blood sugar in 15 minutes, and repeat if it is still low. For an unconscious patient, give glucagon and call 911; never give food or drink.
w: Give a large protein meal and wait an hour.
Give an insulin injection right away.
Give a cup of coffee and go to sleep.
cards.e: This is the 15-15 rule from NIDDK. Glucagon raises blood sugar quickly and is used when a patient cannot safely swallow.

cards.t: What is the treatment for hyperglycemia?
cards.d: Insulin, given as prescribed to lower blood sugar, along with drinking water, checking blood sugar more often, and following the care team's plan. Severe high blood sugar with ketones is a medical emergency that needs immediate care.
w: Eat a large sugary dessert to balance the glucose.
Stop all fluids and wait for the sugar to drop on its own.
Take a sleeping pill and check in the morning.
cards.e: Treatment depends on the type of diabetes. The NIDDK page on insulin describes how the medicine is used to lower high blood sugar.

cards.t: What is the test used to detect both?
cards.d: Blood glucose testing: a fasting plasma glucose test, a random glucose test, or a fingerstick checked with a glucose meter. These show whether blood sugar is too low or too high at that moment.
w: A urine dipstick checked for protein only.
A chest X-ray to look for fluid in the lungs.
A bone density scan of the hip.
cards.e: Glucose testing is the basic way to detect both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia. The A1C test shows average blood sugar over months.

cards.t: What are the symptoms of gestational diabetes?
cards.d: Often there are no symptoms. When present, they can include increased thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, nausea, and blurred vision. Screening is how most cases are found.
w: Severe pain in the lower back that starts after delivery.
A rash on both hands and a loss of hearing.
Bleeding from the gums every morning.
cards.e: Because many people have no symptoms, the CDC recommends screening for gestational diabetes during pregnancy rather than waiting for symptoms.

cards.t: When do the symptoms of hypoglycemia occur?
cards.d: When blood sugar drops below about 70 mg/dL. Common symptoms are shakiness, sweating, fast heartbeat, hunger, dizziness, and confusion; it can happen after missed meals, too much insulin, or exercise.
w: Only after eating a large meal with dessert.
Only when blood sugar is above 300 mg/dL.
Only during sleep when the patient has no insulin in the body.
cards.e: Low blood sugar can come on quickly. Recognizing symptoms early lets the patient treat it before it becomes severe.

cards.t: When do the symptoms of hyperglycemia occur?
cards.d: When blood sugar rises above the target range. Symptoms can include frequent urination, excessive thirst, blurred vision, fatigue, and slow-healing sores, and they become more serious when blood sugar stays very high.
w: Only right after exercise when blood sugar is low.
Only in people who have never eaten sugar.
Only when the patient has a fever of 103 degrees.
cards.e: High blood sugar for a long time causes complications, which is why targets and monitoring matter.

cards.t: What is an insulin auto antibody?
cards.d: An antibody the immune system makes against the body's own insulin. Its presence is a sign of autoimmune type 1 diabetes, and it can appear years before symptoms.
w: A medicine made in a lab to replace insulin in pills.
A type of sugar that the liver stores as energy.
A hormone made by the thyroid to control heart rate.
cards.e: Islet autoantibodies, including insulin autoantibodies, are checked in people at risk of type 1 diabetes.

cards.t: What is a pancreatic β cell diffusion/function?
cards.d: Beta cells are the cells in the pancreas's islets that make and release insulin. Their function is to sense blood glucose and release insulin; when they are damaged, insulin production falls.
w: Beta cells are the red blood cells that carry oxygen to the pancreas.
Beta cells are the kidney filters that remove sugar from urine.
Beta cells are the nerve cells that control hunger in the brain.
cards.e: On the handwritten notes the word reads 'diffusion/function.' This card treats it as beta cell function, the insulin-making role of these cells. Confirm the wording with your instructor.

cards.t: What is hepatic (liver) glucose overproduction?
cards.d: The liver (hepatic) makes and releases too much glucose into the blood, even when glucose is not needed. In type 2 diabetes, insulin does not stop the liver from making extra glucose, which adds to high blood sugar.
w: The liver stops making glucose completely, which causes low blood sugar at night.
The kidneys absorb glucose and send it to the lungs.
The stomach removes all sugar from food before it reaches the blood.
cards.e: The liver normally releases glucose between meals and stops when insulin is present. In type 2 diabetes this control is weaker.

cards.t: How does sugar affect the body?
cards.d: Glucose from food moves into the blood. Insulin lets cells take glucose in for energy. When there is too much sugar in the blood, it damages blood vessels, nerves, and organs over time.
w: Sugar in the blood makes bones grow faster and stronger.
Sugar in the blood cures infections and prevents injury.
Sugar in the blood has no effect on the body if it is not eaten.
cards.e: Cells depend on glucose for energy. Too little causes weakness and confusion; too much harms tissues over the years.

cards.t: How does sugar affect the brain?
cards.d: The brain depends on a steady supply of glucose. Low blood sugar can cause confusion, slurred speech, seizures, or loss of consciousness, and very high blood sugar over time is linked to memory and thinking problems.
w: The brain uses sugar only to make bones, so blood sugar does not change brain function.
Sugar helps the brain only during sleep and has no effect while awake.
The brain makes its own sugar and never needs glucose from the blood.
cards.e: Because the brain stores very little glucose, it needs a steady supply. Severe low blood sugar is a medical emergency.

cards.t: What is the disease for sugar in the body?
cards.d: Diabetes mellitus, a group of diseases in which the body cannot control blood sugar, because insulin is not made enough or is not used well.
w: Hepatitis, an infection of the liver.
Anemia, a shortage of red blood cells.
Asthma, a condition that narrows the airways.
cards.e: Diabetes is the disease that results when blood sugar is not regulated. The main types are type 1, type 2, and gestational diabetes.

cards.t: What is the disease for insulin in the heart/blood?
cards.d: Cardiovascular disease. High blood sugar and insulin resistance damage blood vessels and raise the risk of heart attack, stroke, and heart failure.
w: Pneumonia, an infection of the lungs.
Gout, a build-up of uric acid in the joints.
Glaucoma, high pressure inside the eye.
cards.e: CDC reports that adults with diabetes are about two to four times as likely to die from heart disease or stroke as adults without it.

cards.t: Is diabetes curable (Type 1, Type 2)? Explain.
cards.d: No. Type 1 diabetes cannot be cured, and it needs lifelong insulin. Type 2 diabetes is not curable either, but it can go into remission with weight loss, diet, and exercise, and it is managed with medicine or insulin.
w: Yes, both types are cured by one year of taking vitamin D.
Yes, both types are cured by surgery to remove the pancreas.
Yes, both types disappear once a patient turns 40.
cards.e: Remission means blood sugar stays in the non-diabetes range without medicine. It is possible for some people with type 2, but it is not a cure.

cards.t: What race is most affected and what sex is most affected?
cards.d: American Indian and Alaska Native adults have the highest rate of diagnosed diabetes among race and ethnicity groups in the United States. Men and women are affected at similar rates overall; check the current CDC data for the latest figures.
w: Only people who live in cities are affected, and only women are affected.
Only children are affected, and only boys are affected.
No race or sex is affected more than another, because the disease is not hereditary.
cards.e: Rates vary by age and group. The CDC publishes national statistics on diabetes prevalence by race, ethnicity, and sex, and these should be checked for the newest numbers before using them on an exam.

cards.t: What are the sizes of an insulin syringe?
cards.d: Common insulin syringe sizes are 0.3 mL, 0.5 mL, and 1 mL. The volume is the total liquid the syringe holds, and smaller syringes measure smaller doses more accurately.
w: Insulin syringes come in one size only: 5 mL.
Insulin syringes are measured in feet and inches.
Insulin syringes come in 10 mL, 20 mL, and 50 mL sizes only.
cards.e: FDA clears insulin syringes for use with U-100 insulin. Using the correct syringe size helps prevent dosing errors.

cards.t: Insulin syringes normally come in how many units?
cards.d: Standard U-100 insulin syringes hold 100 units of insulin per mL. The 0.3 mL syringe holds 30 units, the 0.5 mL holds 50 units, and the 1 mL holds 100 units.
w: Insulin syringes come in 10 units per mL.
Insulin syringes come in 500 units per mL.
Insulin syringes come in 1 unit per mL.
cards.e: U-100 means the insulin has 100 units in each mL. Syringes are labeled in units for insulin, not in mL.

cards.t: What are the units, what is a unit?
cards.d: A unit is the measure of insulin strength, not a weight or volume. U-100 insulin has 100 units in each mL, so 10 units is 0.1 mL.
w: A unit is a measure of blood pressure, equal to 10 mmHg.
A unit is one gram of sugar.
A unit is a type of needle used for subcutaneous injections.
cards.e: The unit is set by the insulin's potency. Reading the concentration on the vial, such as U-100, tells you how many units are in each mL.

cards.t: What are the increments of syringes?
cards.d: Most U-100 insulin syringes mark each line at 1 unit, and some marks are 2 units on larger syringes. Doses are drawn to the nearest marked line.
w: Each line is 10 units on every syringe.
Each line is 1 mL on every syringe.
Each line is 100 units on every syringe.
cards.e: The increment on the syringe is printed on the barrel. Always read the markings before drawing up a dose.

cards.t: Insulin units to mL conversion (10, 25, 50, 100 units)
cards.d: For U-100 insulin: 10 units = 0.1 mL, 25 units = 0.25 mL, 50 units = 0.5 mL, and 100 units = 1 mL.
w: 10 units = 1 mL, 25 units = 2.5 mL, 50 units = 5 mL, and 100 units = 10 mL.
10 units = 0.01 mL, 25 units = 0.025 mL, 50 units = 0.05 mL, and 100 units = 0.1 mL.
10 units = 0.5 mL, 25 units = 1 mL, 50 units = 2 mL, and 100 units = 4 mL.
cards.e: Divide the units by 100 to get mL for U-100 insulin. Double-check the vial's concentration before you calculate.

cards.t: When administering insulin, do you pick the syringe according to the dosage size?
cards.d: Yes. Choose the syringe whose size matches the dose, so the dose falls in the upper part of the scale for accuracy.
w: No, the largest syringe is always used to be safe.
No, the syringe size does not matter if the needle is new.
Only if the patient is a child.
cards.e: Using a 1 mL syringe for a 5-unit dose makes it hard to read the amount accurately, which can cause a dosing error.

cards.t: What are the five places you can administer insulin?
cards.d: The abdomen, the front and outer thighs, the upper arms, the buttocks, and the hips or lower back area. Rotate sites within the same area to avoid lumps or thick skin.
w: The palms, the soles of the feet, the scalp, the tongue, and the eyelids.
The fingers, the earlobes, the knees, the heels, and the nose.
The chest, the neck, the armpit, the elbow, and the ankle.
cards.e: Insulin is injected under the skin, where absorption is most consistent. The exact list is taught by the care team and should be checked against the course text.

cards.t: Polyuria
cards.d: Producing a large amount of urine, usually because high blood sugar makes the kidneys pull extra water into the urine.
w: Pain while urinating caused by a stone in the bladder.
A total absence of urine production.
Blood in the urine caused by an injury to the kidney.
cards.e: Polyuria is one of the classic symptoms of high blood sugar, along with polydipsia and weight loss.

cards.t: Polydipsia
cards.d: Excessive thirst. High blood sugar pulls water from the tissues, and the body responds by making the person very thirsty.
w: A fear of drinking water that leads to dehydration.
A condition in which the mouth produces no saliva.
A rash that appears on the lips after eating.
cards.e: Polydipsia and polyuria often occur together with weight loss, fatigue, and blurred vision as signs of high blood sugar.

cards.t: What is a symptom of diabetes in children?
cards.d: Increased thirst and frequent urination, new bedwetting in a child who was previously dry at night, unexplained weight loss, and tiredness.
w: A sudden growth spurt that happens only in adults.
Teeth that become very white and shiny.
Hair that turns gray before age ten.
cards.e: Type 1 diabetes is the most common type diagnosed in children, and its symptoms can appear quickly.

cards.t: If a patient has fruity-smelling breath, what is that a build-up of?
cards.d: Ketones. When the body has too little insulin, it burns fat for fuel and makes ketones, which can cause a fruity smell on the breath. This can signal diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), an emergency.
w: Alcohol from a drink taken earlier in the day.
Mint from toothpaste that was used recently.
Calcium from a diet high in dairy products.
cards.e: Fruity breath with high blood sugar, nausea, or confusion needs urgent medical care because DKA can be life-threatening.

cards.t: What is ED?
cards.d: Erectile dysfunction, the inability to get or keep an erection firm enough for sex. It is more common in men with diabetes.
w: Emergency Department, the hospital unit that treats acute injuries.
Early Detection, a screening program for thyroid disease.
Enzyme Deficiency, a condition that blocks digestion of protein.
cards.e: ED is common in men with diabetes and can be an early sign of blood vessel and nerve damage.

cards.t: How does it (ED) affect men with diabetes?
cards.d: High blood sugar damages the nerves and blood vessels that control erections. Men with diabetes are more likely to develop ED, often earlier in life than men without diabetes.
w: It has no effect because diabetes only affects the eyes.
It makes men unable to produce sperm for life.
It causes a permanent loss of the sense of smell.
cards.e: Treatment options include lifestyle changes, medicines, and counseling. Managing blood sugar lowers the risk of progression.

cards.t: When blood sugars are elevated, vision becomes ___.
cards.d: blurred. High blood sugar causes the lens of the eye to swell, which changes focus, and the blur often goes away when blood sugar returns to the target range.
w: brighter, with colors that look more intense.
completely black in both eyes at all times.
doubled only in the morning and never during the day.
cards.e: Blurred vision from high blood sugar is usually temporary, but long-term high blood sugar can cause permanent eye damage.

cards.t: What is the nerve in the eye affected by diabetes and how does it cause blindness?
cards.d: The retina, the light-sensing layer at the back of the eye, is affected by diabetic retinopathy. High blood sugar damages the tiny blood vessels that feed the retina; they leak, bleed, or grow abnormally, and the damage can cause swelling and scarring that lead to blindness.
w: The cornea, which is damaged when glucose crystallizes on the front of the eye.
The eyelid nerve, which stops blinking and dries the eye out.
The tear duct, which makes the eye produce too little fluid.
cards.e: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of vision loss in adults. The optic nerve can also be affected in some patients. The exact wording of this answer should be checked against your course text.

cards.t: How does diabetes affect the skin?
cards.d: High blood sugar can cause dry, itchy skin, slow wound healing, fungal and bacterial infections, and dark thick patches of skin called acanthosis nigricans, often in the neck or armpits.
w: It makes the skin thicker and resistant to all injuries.
It causes skin to turn bright blue on the arms and legs.
It has no effect because only the eyes and kidneys are affected by diabetes.
cards.e: Poor circulation and nerve damage make infections and foot ulcers more likely. Daily skin and foot checks help catch problems early.

cards.t: What is the name of the organ that produces insulin?
cards.d: The pancreas. Insulin is made by the beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.
w: The liver, which makes insulin in the bile ducts.
The kidneys, which make insulin from filtered sugar.
The spleen, which stores insulin in red blood cells.
cards.e: The pancreas also makes digestive enzymes. Insulin is the hormone it releases to lower blood glucose.

cards.t: What are the causes of gestational diabetes?
cards.d: Hormones made by the placenta during pregnancy make the body less responsive to insulin (insulin resistance). If the pancreas cannot make enough extra insulin to compensate, blood sugar rises. Risk is higher with excess weight, family history, and age.
w: The baby produces sugar in the mother's blood by itself.
Eating sugar causes gestational diabetes in every pregnancy.
Gestational diabetes is caused by a virus that infects the placenta.
cards.e: The exact cause is not fully known. Insulin resistance from pregnancy hormones is the main mechanism, and risk factors add to it.
